summary: Describes the Italian Posta Elettronica Certificata, a certified electronic mail service with legal standing in Italy, recognized in law since the late 1990s and defined in 2005. The document explains how this email-based delivery system is designed. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Certified mail with a stamp from the post office, but for email. It gives you proof it was sent and received, and Italian law accepts that proof.

subtitle: A government-backed certified email system with legal proof of delivery

tldr.problem: Email offers no proof of sending or receiving, but Italian law and business require legally binding confirmation that a message was sent and delivered. End-to-end cryptography requires every user to manage keys and certificates, making it impractical for mainstream adoption.
tldr.mechanism: PEC (Posta Elettronica Certificata) lets ordinary users send email through certified providers that digitally sign messages and generate signed notifications for key events: acceptance by sender's provider, acceptance by receiver's provider, and delivery to the recipient. These notifications provide legal proof.
tldr.outcome: Since 2005, Italian law recognizes PEC messages as legally binding evidence of sending and delivery, widely used by businesses and public administrations for legally binding correspondence.

today: RFC 6109 is an Informational specification that describes the Italian PEC system as defined in 2005 and functioning at the time of publication in 2011. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The system remains in legal use in Italy for certified electronic mail and is recognized by Italian law as providing legally binding proof of sending and delivery. However, the IETF community identified areas where a modern standard would benefit from better alignment with email and security standards.

sections.title: The Need for Certified Email
sections.content:
Regular email has no proof of delivery. You cannot prove to a court that you sent a message or that the recipient received it. While end-to-end cryptography (using PKI and digital signatures) can provide this proof, it requires every user to generate keys, obtain certificates, and understand how to sign and verify messages—a level of technical knowledge that most people lack.

In 1997, Italian law recognized electronic delivery systems as legally usable. By 2005, after technical testing, the Italian government (through DigitPA, the National Center for Informatics in the Public Administration) defined a standard for certified email called PEC. The system uses servers managed by certified providers to sign messages and generate proof of key events: when a message is sent, when it reaches the recipient's provider, and when it is delivered to the recipient's mailbox. Users only need a standard email client.
sections.plainLanguage: Email is like talking on the phone—no record of it happening. PEC is like certified mail: the post office stamps it and gives you receipts. Italian law trusts those receipts.

sections.title: System Architecture and Participants
sections.content:
PEC operates as a network of certified providers, each managing their own PEC domains (like a company's email domain). A PEC message travels through three main points within each provider: the Access Point (where the user submits), the Incoming Point (where messages arrive from other providers), and the Delivery Point (where the recipient's mailbox lives).

When a user sends a message, the Access Point checks it, signs a server-user acceptance notification, and wraps the original message in a PEC transport envelope. The message goes to the recipient's provider's Incoming Point, which verifies the signature and sends back a server-server acceptance notification (for inter-provider communication only). Finally, the Delivery Point checks the message and delivers it to the recipient, sending a delivery notification back to the sender as proof.
sections.plainLanguage: PEC has three checkpoints: sending provider accepts it, receiving provider accepts it, recipient gets it. Each checkpoint sends a signed receipt.

sections.title: Message Format and Digital Signing
sections.content:
PEC uses S/MIME (Secure/MIME) and CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) to sign all system-generated messages. The original user message is wrapped in a PEC transport envelope, and both the envelope and all notifications are signed with the provider's private key. The X.509v3 certificate associated with the key is included so that recipients can verify the signature.

System-generated messages include special header fields like X-Ricevuta (indicating notification type) and X-Riferimento-Message-ID (linking to the original message). All notifications include a human-readable text part explaining what happened and an XML part containing certification data: the sender and recipient addresses, the timestamp, the message subject, and a message identifier. The XML data and signatures provide the legal proof that the message was processed at specific times by the provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Each receipt is a signed email. The signature proves the provider (not a hacker) created it. The XML part has the exact date, time, sender, and recipient.

sections.title: Notifications and Proof Chain
sections.content:
PEC generates different notifications for different events. A server-user acceptance notification confirms that the sender's provider accepted the message. A delivery notification confirms that the message reached the recipient's mailbox. If something goes wrong—formal errors in the message or virus detection—the provider sends a non-delivery notification explaining why.

Delay notifications inform the user if a message has not been accepted or delivered within 12 hours, and another delay notification at 24 hours if still pending. This chain of signed notifications provides a complete timeline for legal purposes: proof of when the message left the sender's system, when the receiving provider took responsibility for it, and when the recipient was able to retrieve it. Timestamps are critical; PEC uses digital timestamps to ensure the date and time cannot be repudiated.
sections.plainLanguage: You get a receipt when the provider sends it, another when the other provider gets it, and a final one when the recipient's mail arrives. If anything goes wrong, you get a receipt for that too.

sections.title: Security and Provider Directory
sections.content:
PEC providers must be registered and trustworthy. The system maintains an LDAP directory of certified providers, storing each provider's X.509 certificate, the domains they manage, and a hash of the certificate for efficient lookup. Incoming messages are verified by checking that they are signed by a known provider whose certificate is in the directory and has not been revoked. The system checks Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) to ensure certificates have not been compromised.

For ordinary email (non-PEC) entering the system, virus scanning is performed at the Incoming Point. If a virus is detected in a valid PEC envelope, the receiving provider sends a virus notification to the sending provider, which can then alert the original sender. Additionally, implementations must support key rotation, allowing operators to change authentication keys periodically without disrupting service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider has a certificate to prove who they are. The directory lists all trusted providers. If a message is signed by someone not in the directory, it is treated as ordinary email.

sections.title: Limitations and Legal Status
sections.content:
PEC differs from end-to-end cryptography in a crucial way: it provides proof that a certified provider processed the message, but not end-to-end encryption or confidentiality. The message itself is not encrypted; instead, the provider's signatures prove the message's authenticity and the timestamps of key events.

RFC 6109 is an Informational document describing an existing Italian system. It represents the specifications as they stood in 2011 (based on Italian law DPR from November 2005). The IETF noted that the specification has some design choices that differ from traditional email standards, and a modern update would need to address alignment with IETF terminology and standards. Nonetheless, the system has legal standing in Italy and is widely deployed for business and government correspondence.
sections.plainLanguage: PEC doesn't hide the message like encryption does. It just proves who sent it and when. That's enough for the law, and it's simpler than cryptography for everyone.
